content.prompt: In the diagram below, $\triangle X'Y'Z'$ is the image under translation of $\triangle XYZ$. Copy the diagram onto your graph paper.

spec.mathematics: Using the lower-left grid corner as (0,0): X=(4,8), Y=(1,3), Z=(6,3), X'=(14,6), Y'=(11,1), Z'=(16,1). Translation: 10 units right and 2 units down. Each triangle has base 5 units and perpendicular height 5 units.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Measure angles $XYZ$ and $X'Y'Z'$ with your protractor. What do you notice?

answer.short: Both angles are approximately $59^\circ$. They are the same size.
answer.worked: Place the protractor centre at $Y$, with its baseline along $YZ$, and read the angle to $YX$: approximately $59^\circ$. Repeat at $Y'$ with the baseline along $Y'Z'$: approximately $59^\circ$. Corresponding angles are equal under translation.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Write down the angle in the image that is the same size as each angle below. (Check with a protractor.)

answer.short: $\angle X'Z'Y'$
answer.worked: $X$, $Z$ and $Y$ correspond to $X'$, $Z'$ and $Y'$, respectively. Thus $\angle XZY=\angle X'Z'Y'$. A protractor check gives approximately $68^\circ$ for each.

answer.short: $\angle Z'X'Y'$
answer.worked: $Z$, $X$ and $Y$ correspond to $Z'$, $X'$ and $Y'$, respectively. Thus $\angle ZXY=\angle Z'X'Y'$. A protractor check gives approximately $53^\circ$ for each.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Accurately measure the lengths of the intervals $XY$ and $X'Y'$. Comment.

answer.short: $XY$ and $X'Y'$ have the same length.
answer.worked: Align the ruler's zero with $X$ and measure to $Y$. Repeat from $X'$ to $Y'$. The measurements agree: translation preserves length.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Calculate the area, in square units, of $\triangle XYZ$ and $\triangle X'Y'Z'$. Comment.

answer.short: Both areas are $12.5$ square units. The areas are equal.
answer.worked:
Each triangle has a base of $5$ units and a perpendicular height of $5$ units.
$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{Area}(\triangle XYZ)&=\tfrac12\times5\times5\\\operatorname{Area}(\triangle XYZ)&=12.5\text{ square units}\\\operatorname{Area}(\triangle X'Y'Z')&=\tfrac12\times5\times5\\\operatorname{Area}(\triangle X'Y'Z')&=12.5\text{ square units}\end{align*}$$
The areas are equal.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the area of $ABCE$ and $A'B'C'E'$ in square units. Comment.

answer.short: Both areas are $12$ square units. Rotation preserves area.
answer.worked:
The rectangular body $ABCE$ is $4$ units wide and $3$ units high. Its image has the same side lengths.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area of }ABCE&=4\times3\\\text{Area of }ABCE&=12\text{ square units}\\\text{Area of }A'B'C'E'&=3\times4\\\text{Area of }A'B'C'E'&=12\text{ square units}\end{align*}$$
The areas are equal: rotation preserves area.

spec.mathematics: Rotate every vertex about the marked centre while preserving its radius.

answer.short: $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about the marked centre.
answer.worked:
Rotate each vertex two $30^\circ$ divisions anticlockwise and join the images. Then rotate those vertices one further division anticlockwise and join them. Each vertex stays on its original circle.

$$60^\circ+30^\circ=90^\circ.$$

The single rotation is $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about the marked centre. In the diagram, blue is the original, red is the first image and green is the final image.

answer.short: $30^\circ$ clockwise about the marked centre.
answer.worked:
Rotate each vertex one $30^\circ$ division anticlockwise and join the images. Then rotate the first image two divisions clockwise, keeping each vertex the same distance from the centre.

The second turn reverses the first $30^\circ$ and continues a further $30^\circ$ clockwise. The single rotation is therefore $30^\circ$ clockwise about the marked centre.

In the diagram, blue is the original, red is the first image and green is the final image.

Rotate each vertex four $30^\circ$ divisions anticlockwise. The vertices exchange positions, so the first image has the same outline as the original triangle. Rotate that image a further three divisions anticlockwise.

$$120^\circ+90^\circ=210^\circ.$$

The single rotation is $210^\circ$ anticlockwise about the marked centre. The dashed red first image coincides with the blue original; green shows the final image.

children.label: a
children.prompt: For each letter and symbol, mark any axes of symmetry.

answer.short: Vertical axis only: A, M, T, U, V, W, Y. Horizontal axis only: B, C, D, E, K. Horizontal and vertical axes: H, I, O, X, =. Four axes: + (horizontal, vertical and both diagonals). No axes: F, G, J, L, N, P, Q, R, S, Z, $\$$, %. These answers depend on the drawn forms.
answer.worked:
Reflect each figure in a proposed line. Keep the line only when the reflected figure fits exactly onto the original.

A, M, T, U, V, W and Y have a vertical axis. B, C, D, E and K have a horizontal axis. H, I, O, X and = have horizontal and vertical axes. The equal-armed + has horizontal, vertical and two diagonal axes. F, G, J, L, N, P, Q, R, S, Z, $\$$ and % have no reflection axes in the intended forms.

The result can change with the lettering: unequal lobes of B remove its horizontal axis; a circular O has every diameter as an axis; a square-proportioned X can have two additional diagonal axes.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Does each figure have rotational symmetry? If so, mark the centre of the rotation on the diagram. State the order of rotational symmetry.

answer.short: Order 2: H, I, N, O, S, X, Z, =, $\$$, %. Order 4: +. All remaining figures have order 1. Mark the centre of each order-2 or order-4 figure at its centre of rotation.
answer.worked:
Turn each figure about its centre and count the positions in one complete turn where it fits exactly onto itself, including the final full turn.

H, I, N, O, S, X, Z, =, $\$$ and % fit after a half-turn and a full turn, so their order is 2. Their smallest matching rotation is $360^{\circ}/2=180^{\circ}$. Mark the common centre of these rotations; for % this is midway between its two loops, and for = it is midway between the two bars.

The equal-armed + fits after $90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$, so its order is 4. Its centre is the intersection of the arms.

A, B, C, D, E, F, G, J, K, L, M, P, Q, R, T, U, V, W and Y fit only after a full turn, so they have order 1 and no nontrivial rotational symmetry.

These results require the intended symmetric glyphs: for example, a circular O has infinitely many matching rotations, while unequal lobes of S or unequal loops of % can remove half-turn symmetry.

Each axis must reflect the whole figure exactly onto itself.

Square: the two diagonals and the two lines joining opposite side midpoints.

Rectangle: the horizontal and vertical lines through its centre.

Rhombus: both diagonals.

Kite: the diagonal joining the vertices where equal sides meet, vertical in the drawing.

Equilateral triangle: each line through a vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side.

Isosceles triangle: the line through the apex and the midpoint of its base.

The unequal-legged right triangle, the given trapezium and the given parallelogram have no reflection axes.

answer.short:
Square: 4. Rectangle: 2. Rhombus: 2. Kite: 1. Equilateral triangle: 3. Isosceles triangle: 1. Right triangle: 1. Trapezium: 1. Circle: infinite. Ellipse: 2. Parallelogram: 2.

Order 1 means no rotational symmetry other than a full turn. Mark the geometric centre for each figure of order greater than 1.
answer.worked:
The order counts the positions in one full turn at which the figure fits exactly onto itself.

Square: the smallest rotation is $90^\circ$, so its order is $360^\circ/90^\circ=4$; the centre is the intersection of its diagonals.

Rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram: a $180^\circ$ turn works, giving order $360^\circ/180^\circ=2$; mark the intersection of the diagonals.

Equilateral triangle: a $120^\circ$ turn works, giving order $360^\circ/120^\circ=3$; mark the intersection of its medians.

Ellipse: a $180^\circ$ turn works, giving order 2; mark the intersection of its major and minor axes.

Circle: every rotation about its centre works, so its order is infinite.

The kite, non-equilateral isosceles triangle, unequal-legged right triangle and given trapezium fit again only after $360^\circ$. Their order is 1, so they have no non-trivial rotational symmetry.

answer.short: 36 and 37, respectively.
answer.worked:
A regular polygon with $n$ sides fits exactly onto itself after each rotation of $\frac{360^\circ}{n}$ about its centre. There are $n$ such positions in a full turn, so its rotational symmetry has order $n$.

The regular 36-gon has order 36, and the regular 37-gon has order 37.

answer.short:
One possible pair is $\ell_1:x=2$ and $\ell_2:x=4$. There are infinitely many possible pairs. The distance between the lines is $2$ units.

Use parallel vertical axes, with the second axis $2$ units to the right of the first.
answer.worked:
Plot and join $A(0,0)$, $B(2,0)$, $C(2,4)$, then plot and join $A'(4,0)$, $B'(6,0)$, $C'(6,4)$.

Choose $\ell_1:x=2$. Reflect each vertex horizontally, placing its image the same distance on the opposite side of this line. The intermediate vertices are $(4,0)$, $(2,0)$ and $(2,4)$.

Choose $\ell_2:x=4$. Reflect the intermediate vertices in this line. They become $(4,0)$, $(6,0)$ and $(6,4)$, as required. A vertex on an axis stays fixed.

The translation is $4$ units right. Two reflections in parallel vertical lines produce a horizontal translation twice their separation, so the lines must be $2$ units apart, with the second to the right of the first. Both lines can be shifted horizontally together, giving infinitely many possible pairs.

content.prompt: The triangle $ABC$ whose vertices have coordinates $A(0,0)$, $B(2,0)$, $C(2,4)$ is translated to the triangle $A'B'C'$ with coordinates $A'(0,4)$, $B'(2,4)$, $C'(2,8)$. Draw the two triangles on a number plane and draw in two axes of reflection, $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$, such that when triangle $ABC$ is reflected in $\ell_1$ and its image is reflected in $\ell_2$, the final result is triangle $A'B'C'$. Is there only one way to do this? What is the distance between lines $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$?

answer.short:
For example, $\ell_1:y=3$ and $\ell_2:y=5$. No; there are many possible pairs. The distance between the lines is $2$ units.

Reflect in the lower horizontal line first, then in the upper line, which is $2$ units above it.
answer.worked:
One choice is $\ell_1:y=3$ followed by $\ell_2:y=5$.

Reflect each vertex in $\ell_1$, placing its image the same perpendicular distance on the other side. The intermediate vertices are $(0,6)$, $(2,6)$ and $(2,2)$.

Reflect these vertices in $\ell_2$. Their images are $A'(0,4)$, $B'(2,4)$ and $C'(2,8)$, as required. Join the corresponding vertices to form the triangles.

The axes are $5-3=2$ units apart. There are many choices: any horizontal first axis and a second horizontal axis $2$ units above it give the same translation of $4$ units upwards.

children.prompt: Draw two lines $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ through $O$ such that, when triangle $ABC$ is reflected in $\ell_1$ and its image is reflected in $\ell_2$, the final result is triangle $A'B'C'$.

answer.short: One possible construction is shown: $\ell_1$ slopes upwards to the right at $45^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, and $\ell_2$ is vertical. Reflect in $\ell_1$ first, then in $\ell_2$.
answer.worked: Draw a vertical line $\ell_2$ through $O$ and a line $\ell_1$ through $O$ sloping upwards to the right at $45^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. Reflect each vertex of $ABC$ in $\ell_1$, placing its image at the same perpendicular distance on the other side. Join these vertices to form the intermediate triangle. No. There are many possible pairs of axes through $O$.

The acute angle must be $45^{\circ}$, with the reflections ordered to produce the anticlockwise rotation.

entries.description:
We will be dealing with only three types of transformation in this chapter:
1 translations (diagram 1)
2 rotations (diagram 2)
3 reflections (diagram 3).
Note that none of these transformations changes the size or shape of an object.
You will have seen these three transformations in many applications on your computer.
All of these transformations satisfy two important properties.

entries.description:
A rotation turns a figure about a fixed point, called the centre of rotation. The centre of rotation is usually labelled by the letter O.
A rotation is specified by:
• the centre of rotation O
• the angle of rotation
• the direction of rotation (clockwise or anticlockwise).

The examples above demonstrate the following special properties of any rotation.
The identity rotation is the rotation that rotates a figure through 0° and leaves every point fixed.

entries.description:
Properties of rotations
For any non-identity rotation:
• every interval is rotated to an interval of equal length
• every angle is rotated to an angle of equal size
• there is only one fixed point – the centre of rotation
• the distance of a point from the centre of rotation does not change.

entries.description: A reflection is a transformation that flips a figure about a line. This line is called the axis of reflection. A good way to understand this is to suppose that you have a book with clear plastic pages and a figure drawn, as in the picture below. If the page is turned, the triangle is flipped over. We say it has been reflected; in this case, the axis of reflection is the binding of the book.

entries.description:
When a reflection is applied:
• all points on the axis of reflection are fixed points; the only fixed points are those on the axis of reflection
• if the points A, B, C, … are in a clockwise order, then the points A′, B′, C′, … will be in anticlockwise order, and vice versa
• if a reflection is applied twice, all figures are returned to their original position
• every interval is reflected to an interval of equal length
• every angle is reflected to an angle of equal size.

entries.description: Symmetry is an important idea in mathematics. We also see it in art and architecture. Here we are going to consider two types of symmetry, namely rotational symmetry and reflection symmetry.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone topic introduction; retained as teaching evidence and excluded from practice-only authoring.

entries.description: The figure shown opposite has reflection symmetry because it falls back exactly on itself when it is reflected in the axis of reflection marked on the diagram. This line is called an axis of symmetry of the figure.
entries.presentation: Text on the left, with the associated face diagram on the right.

entries.description:
Think of rotating the figure shown opposite by 90° anticlockwise about O. The figure moves back on top of the original figure where A has moved to where B was, B has moved to where C was, C has moved to where D was, and D has moved to where A was. We say that the figure has rotational symmetry.

Next we look at the situation after repeated anticlockwise rotations of 90°. For example, the original point A in diagram 1 moves to the point A in diagram 2. It then moves to the point A in diagram 3, and so on.
entries.presentation: Explanatory text on the left; Diagram 1 on the right. Diagrams 2–5 follow in a two-column, two-row arrangement.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone rotational-symmetry demonstration; its imperative wording does not constitute a practice question.

A separate blue curved arrow outside the upper-right quadrant indicates anticlockwise rotation.

entries.description:
You can see that it takes four rotations of (360/4)° = 90° anticlockwise for the point A to return to its original position.

We say that our figure has rotational symmetry of order 4:
• 90° is the smallest angle of rotation that makes it fit exactly on top of itself, and
• when we repeat this rotation four times, we get the identity rotation of 360°.

entries.description:
Symmetry of regular polygons
Regular polygons have a lot of symmetry. For example, the regular pentagon has five axes of reflection symmetry, as shown in the diagram opposite.
As we rotate the pentagon about the centre O, every 72° it will ‘fall back on itself’, looking identical to the original diagram even though the points have moved. The five rotations 72°, 144°, 216°, 288°, 360° about the centre O are symmetries.
Thus the regular pentagon has rotational symmetry of order 5.

entries.description:
Follow the steps below to construct a regular hexagon without using a protractor.

Draw a circle of radius 5 cm. Leave your compasses set at 5 cm and mark a point A on the circle.

Place the point of your compasses on A and mark an arc intersecting the circle at B. Move the point of your compasses to B and mark an arc intersecting the circle at C. Continue around the circle.

To check your accuracy, draw a final arc centred at F. It should pass through A. As before, join the points A, B, C, D, E and F to form a regular hexagon.
